title: 2014_PMC5779422_Human_papillomavirus_vaccination_coverage_among_adolescents_2007
ehr_evidence: CDC analyzed data from the 2007–2013 National Immunization Survey-Teen (NIS-Teen) and national postlicensure vaccine safety data among females and males; NIS-Teen uses a random-digit-dialed sample with a questionnaire mailed to each provider to obtain a vaccination history from medical records, and safety data came from the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS).
summary: A cross-sectional, survey-based MMWR report analyzing HPV vaccination coverage among US adolescents aged 13–17 years (2007–2013) via NIS-Teen and postlicensure safety via VAERS.
key_findings: HPV vaccination coverage with ≥1 dose increased significantly from 53.8% (2012) to 57.3% (2013) among girls and from 20.8% (2012) to 34.6% (2013) among boys.
Among girls, receipt of ≥1 dose of HPV by age 13 years increased an average of 5.9% (95% CI = 2.8%–9.0%) with each new birth cohort, reaching 46.8% (CI = 41.2%–52.5%) for the 2000 birth cohort.

If all missed opportunities for HPV vaccination had been eliminated for the 2000 birth cohort, coverage with ≥1 dose could have reached 91.3% (CI = 87.9%–93.8%) by age 13 years, a 42.7 percentage-point difference.
The percentage of parents reporting a clinician HPV vaccine recommendation was significantly higher in 2013 than 2012 for parents of girls (64.4% vs 61.0%) and parents of boys (41.6% vs 28.0%).
VAERS received 25,176 adverse event reports after HPV vaccination (June 2006–March 2014), of which 92.4% of HPV4 reports were classified as nonserious.
captured_features: HPV vaccination coverage estimates by dose and survey year
clinician HPV vaccine recommendation to parents
study_design: cross-sectional survey (with birth-cohort analysis) plus passive safety surveillance
data_source_type: survey (NIS-Teen) and passive adverse-event reporting system (VAERS)
population: US adolescents aged 13–17 years (girls and boys), 2007–2013
limitations: Low household response rates (landline 51.1%, cell phone 23.3%), with residual nonresponse/noncoverage bias possible.
Provider-reported vaccination histories may be incomplete, contributing to underestimation of coverage.
VAERS is a passive reporting system that cannot establish cause and effect and is subject to underreporting and reporting bias.
